description: Evidence-based mood-to-nutrient mapping with enhanced scientific accuracy and safe claim wording
changelog: v2.2.0 - Enhanced evidence levels, added Vitamin D/Zinc/Selenium, improved safe claim wording, aligned with clinical guidelines

moods.description: Feeling anxious, stressed, or unable to relax

nutrients.name: magnesium
nutrients.note: helps the body cope with stress

nutrients.name: omega_3_epa_dha
nutrients.note: anti-inflammatory properties, may support mood balance

nutrients.name: fiber
nutrients.note: supports gut-brain axis health

nutrients.name: vitamin_d
nutrients.note: supports overall health and may play a role in mood balance

nutrients.name: zinc
nutrients.note: essential mineral for brain and nervous system support

nutrients.name: added_sugar
nutrients.note: limit to avoid blood sugar spikes that may worsen stress

explainers: Magnesium-rich foods (leafy greens, nuts, legumes, whole grains) may be linked to calmer mood in several studies, particularly when deficiency exists.
EPA-rich omega-3 sources (salmon, mackerel, sardines) show small-to-modest effects for anxiety reduction in meta-analyses when EPA ≥ 60% of EPA+DHA.
Mediterranean dietary pattern with anti-inflammatory focus shows observational and some RCT support for stress reduction.
Limiting caffeine and refined sugars may help prevent stress-amplifying blood sugar swings.
moods.evidence: Meta-analyses show magnesium and omega-3 may have small-to-moderate benefits for anxiety, with variable results across studies. Benefits are most pronounced when deficiency exists. Mediterranean pattern shows consistent stress reduction benefits.
moods.evidence_level: Low-Moderate - Observational links, some trials in stress/anxiety, but mixed results

moods.description: Feeling physically or mentally exhausted, lacking energy

nutrients.name: iron
nutrients.note: iron-supportive foods help with energy when levels are adequate

nutrients.name: vitamin_c
nutrients.note: may enhance non-heme iron absorption

nutrients.name: complex_carbs
nutrients.note: may provide sustained energy release

nutrients.name: fiber
nutrients.note: may help prevent energy crashes

nutrients.name: protein
nutrients.note: may help sustain energy levels

nutrients.name: vitamin_b12
nutrients.note: important for brain function and energy metabolism

nutrients.name: folate
nutrients.note: important for brain function and emotional balance

nutrients.name: vitamin_b6
nutrients.note: important for brain function and emotional balance

explainers: Iron deficiency (even without anemia) is well-established cause of fatigue, cognitive difficulties, and irritability. Clinical improvement seen when deficiency is corrected.
Iron-supportive recipes emphasize both heme (lean red meat) and non-heme (spinach, legumes, fortified grains) sources paired with vitamin C for enhanced absorption.
Complex carbohydrates with fiber provide steady energy without crashes.
Protein helps maintain stable blood sugar and sustained energy throughout the day.
moods.evidence: Iron deficiency is a well-established cause of fatigue, even in the absence of anemia. Food-first iron intake with vitamin C co-factors is recommended by WHO and medical guidelines.
moods.evidence_level: Moderate-Strong - Clinical guidelines, RCTs show benefit when deficient
key_studies: Iron deficiency and fatigue (Office of Dietary Supplements)

nutrients.name: added_sugar
nutrients.note: limit as high sugar intake may be linked to mood swings

explainers: Mediterranean dietary pattern with anti-inflammatory focus shows observational and some RCT support for depression improvement (SMILES trial).
EPA-rich omega-3 sources (≥60% EPA of EPA+DHA) show small-to-modest effect sizes for depressive symptoms in meta-analyses.
High-fiber, plant-rich meals support beneficial gut bacteria, which influence mood through the gut-brain axis.
B-vitamins (folate, B6, B12) show correlations with mood but limited high-quality RCTs - treat as supportive building blocks.
moods.evidence: STRONGEST - The SMILES trial demonstrated significant depression symptom reduction with Mediterranean diet intervention. Multiple meta-analyses support omega-3 and fiber benefits.
moods.evidence_level: Low-Moderate - Small effect in RCTs/meta-analyses, best in those with inflammation or depression
key_studies: SMILES trial (2017) - Mediterranean diet for depression

nutrients.name: vitamin_b12

explainers: Protein and fiber together stabilize blood sugar, preventing the mood swings and irritability that come from glucose spikes and crashes.
Reducing added sugar eliminates a major trigger for blood sugar instability.
Ultra-processed foods are associated with worse mood outcomes; whole foods support emotional balance.
Omega-3 fatty acids have anti-inflammatory properties that may help reduce agitation.
moods.evidence: Ultra-processed food consumption correlates with mood disturbances. Glycemic stability through protein and fiber helps prevent irritability associated with blood sugar swings.
moods.evidence_level: Low-Moderate - Deficiency linked with depression/irritability; supplementation helps if deficient

mediterranean_base.description: Mediterranean dietary pattern with anti-inflammatory focus - whole foods, antioxidants, neuroprotective herbs/spices
mediterranean_base.practical_guidance: Focus on anti-oxidant, anti-inflammatory foods. Use herbs/spices (e.g. turmeric) with known neuroprotective potential.

low_ultra_processed.description: Minimize ultra-processed foods which correlate with worse mood

limit_high_caffeine.description: Moderate caffeine to avoid anxiety spikes

stabilize_glycemia.description: Protein and fiber slow glucose absorption, preventing mood-disrupting blood sugar swings

disclaimers.general: This app provides food suggestions based on mood and nutritional science. It is not a substitute for professional medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always seek the advice of your physician or other qualified health provider with any questions you may have regarding a medical condition.
disclaimers.iron: If you experience persistent fatigue, consider getting tested for iron deficiency before significantly increasing iron intake. People with hemochromatosis or iron overload should avoid high-iron recommendations. Iron-supportive recipes emphasize both heme (animal) and non-heme (plant) sources paired with vitamin C.
disclaimers.b_vitamins: B-vitamins are important for brain function and may support mood when levels are adequate. Benefits are most pronounced in deficiency states. Consult a healthcare provider if you suspect deficiency.
disclaimers.supplements: This app recommends food-first approaches. Consult a healthcare provider before taking supplements.
disclaimers.persistent_symptoms: If mood symptoms persist or worsen, please consult a mental health professional.
disclaimers.evidence_disclaimer: The strength of evidence varies by mood. Mediterranean diet shows observational and some RCT support. Omega-3 EPA shows small-to-modest effects in meta-analyses. Iron deficiency is well-established for fatigue. Other micronutrients show correlations but limited high-quality RCTs. Treat recommendations as supportive building blocks, not cure-alls.
disclaimers.omega3_epa: Omega-3 recommendations focus on EPA-rich sources (≥60% EPA of EPA+DHA) based on meta-analyses showing small-to-modest effects for mood support. Include oily fish, flaxseeds, chia seeds as supportive elements.
disclaimers.micronutrients: B-vitamins, magnesium, zinc, selenium, vitamin D show observational correlations with mood but limited high-quality RCTs. Use whole-food ingredients rich in these nutrients as supportive building blocks rather than standalone treatments.

removed_moods_note: Version 2.0.0 removed 8 moods (dreamy, focused, playful, craving, light, grounded, restorative, charismatic) due to insufficient scientific evidence linking these emotional states to specific nutrient needs. Focus is now exclusively on evidence-based recommendations.
